newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa in low gear, year on from macro-plan.
newsitem.headline: South Africa in low gear, year on from macro-plan.

text.p: Investor confidence and foreign funds are returning to South Africa, spurred in large part by a conservative macroeconomic strategy which is one year old this week.
But for ordinary South Africans, especially the unemployed, there is little to celebrate.

The five-year Growth, Employment and Redistribution (Gear) strategy, unveiled last June 14, seeks to lift growth to six percent and create 400,000 new jobs a year by 2000. One year on, the real economy's performance has proved weaker than expected.
GDP growth in 1996 was 3.1 percent rather than the 3.5 percent targeted and officials acknowledge that the 1997 goal of 2.9 percent will not be met.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Wednesday he thought the economy could still expand by 2.5 percent this year, but many economists expect less than two percent after a surprise 0.8 percent drop in first quarter growth.

Most worryingly, Gear's job-creation hopes look increasingly vulnerable. The plan envisaged job growth in the non-agricultural formal sector of 1.3 percent in 1996. In fact, employment fell by 1.1 percent, according to the Reserve Bank's economics department.
Few economists see any prospect of this year's goal of 3.0 percent jobs growth being met.

Nico Czypionka, chief economist at Standard Bank, believes the employment figures contained in Gear were never realistic. Planned cuts in the budget deficit made public sector job losses inevitable while private firms had to lay off workers to compete in the face of lower import tariffs.

"What one would expect from an economy that is rationalising to increase dynamics is, in the short term, a reduction in jobs rather than an increase -- particularly when government itself is committed to reducing numbers," he said.
Raymond Parsons, director-general of the South African Chamber of Business, said the employment goals in Gear were its weakest link.
"The job targets have been too ambitious, given the recent mixture of tariff reform, currency depreciation and a malfunctioning labour market," he wrote in Business Day this week.

Gear calls for "greater flexibility" in the labour market to address unemployment running at around 33 percent, but is short on specifics. Hopes are now pinned on a proposed "jobs summit" to boost employment incentives and sooth strained relations between business and labour in the wake of a one-day general strike earlier this month over workers' rights.

The average South African may not have felt the benefits, but economists are impressed by the government's progress in reducing the budget deficit, easing exchange controls and implementing supply-side measures to boost exports.
Manuel's March 12 budget cut the fiscal deficit from 5.1 to 4.0 percent of GDP, as promised, and his proposals on exchange controls went considerably further than many had expected.

A tight monetary stance is also delivering results, with inflation now peaking and likely to average less than the 9.7 percent forecast in Gear for 1997. Deputy Finance Minister Gill Marcus this month predicted a figure of 9.5 percent.
That should allow for lower interest rates later this year, paving the way for an upturn in 1998, although the rate of reduction will once again be slower than hoped.
Gear had projected a real Bank rate of 5.0 percent this year and 4.0 percent in 1998, after allowing for inflation. Halfway through 1997, it still stands at over seven percent.
Despite the shortfalls, Sandra Gordon, economist at fund manager Syfrets in Cape Town, argues the strategy offers investors policy certainty which will yield results in time.
